blocks.text:
A container is not a kernel object. The Linux kernel has no data structure named "container". What is called a container is an ordinary process (or a tree of processes) whose view of the system has been narrowed by **namespaces**, whose resource consumption has been bounded by **control groups** (cgroups), and whose root file system has been replaced by an image mounted through a **union file system**. Docker, containerd, CRI-O and Kubernetes automate the assembly of these three kernel features and add distribution, scheduling and lifecycle management on top.

This distinction determines how containers fail in production. A Spring Boot service in a pod still uses the host kernel, the host scheduler, the host page cache and the host network stack. A memory limit is enforced by the kernel out-of-memory killer, a CPU limit by the CFS bandwidth controller, and a process that ignores SIGTERM is terminated by the same signal rules as on a bare host. A diagnosis therefore starts from the Linux mechanisms described in the earlier Parts, applied to the cgroup that contains the process.

The chapter derives containers from the three kernel features, builds one by hand with `unshare` and `chroot`, measures the limits with a memory cgroup and a CPU quota on the build machine, and closes with the mapping from Kubernetes requests and limits to cgroup files and to the out-of-memory score.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Namespaces: what a process can see

A namespace wraps a global kernel resource so that the processes inside observe a private instance of it. The kernel provides eight types. Each process belongs to exactly one namespace of each type; the membership is visible as symbolic links under `/proc/PID/ns/`.

rows: Own PID numbering; the first process is PID 1 and acts as init.
Private mount table; a mount made inside is invisible outside.
Own hostname and NIS domain name.
Own System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues.
Own interfaces, routing table, firewall rules and port space.
Own UID/GID mapping; root inside may be an unprivileged UID outside.
Own view of the cgroup hierarchy root.
Own offsets for the monotonic and boot clocks.
blocks.caption: Namespace types and the resource each one isolates.

blocks.text: A namespace is created with `clone()` flags at process creation, with `unshare()` for the calling process, or joined with `setns()`. The `nsenter` command joins the namespaces of an existing process, which is how `docker exec` and `kubectl` `exec` place a shell inside a running container.

blocks.caption: Namespaces are identified by inode numbers: the container created with unshare shares the user and cgroup namespaces with the host but owns new pid, mnt, uts, ipc and net namespaces.
blocks.alt: Namespace Host (initial namespace) Container (after unshare) Isolates | pid 4026531836 4026532276 process IDs; PID 1 | mnt 4026531832 4026532273 mount table | uts 4026531838 4026532274 hostname | ipc 4026531839 4026532275 SysV IPC, queues | net 4026531833 4026532277 interfaces, ports | user 4026531837 (shared) UID/GID mapping | cgroup 4026531835 (shared) cgroup root view | Inode numbers read from /proc/PID/ns/* on the build machine; orange = new namespace created for the container

blocks.text: The pid namespace deserves particular attention because it changes the meaning of process identity. A process has one PID per namespace level in which it is visible. The same task is PID 1275 in the host namespace and PID 1 inside the container; the field `NSpid` in `/proc/PID/status` lists both values. Signals sent from the host with the host PID reach the task; the task cannot see or signal host processes at all.

blocks.text:
#### Control groups: how much a process can use

A cgroup is a node in a tree to which processes are attached and on which controllers enforce limits and accounting. The memory controller limits resident memory and page cache, the cpu controller limits and weights CPU time, the pids controller limits the number of tasks, and the blkio (v1) or io (v2) controller limits block device bandwidth.

Two interface generations coexist in the field. In **cgroup v1** each controller owns a separate hierarchy mounted under `/sys/fs/cgroup/<controller>/`. In **cgroup v2** there is a single unified hierarchy at `/sys/fs/cgroup/` and every controller appears as files in the same directory. The build machine used for the experiments in this Part runs a hybrid layout: v1 controller mounts plus a v2 mount at `/sys/fs/cgroup/unified` (`stat -fc %T` reports `cgroup2fs` for it). Linux 6.18 and JDK 21 were used throughout.

blocks.text:
#### Union file systems: what a process sees as its root

An image is a stack of read-only layers. A container adds one writable layer and presents the union as a single directory tree. Linux implements this with **overlayfs**: `lowerdir` holds the read-only layers, `upperdir` holds the writable layer, `workdir` is scratch space, and the mount exposes the union. A write to a file that exists only in a lower layer first **copies** **the whole file up** to the upper layer. A deletion creates a **whiteout**, a character device with major and minor number 0, in the upper layer.

blocks.text:
Copy-up has a performance consequence: appending one byte to a 2 GB file in a lower layer first copies 2 GB. Databases and large log files therefore belong on a volume, which is a bind mount outside overlayfs, rather than in the writable layer.

#### Docker architecture and the runtime chain

The `docker` command is a client of the `dockerd` daemon through a REST API. `dockerd` manages images and networks and delegates container lifecycle to `containerd`. For each container `containerd` starts a `containerd-shim` process, which stays alive as the parent of the container process and holds its standard streams. The shim invokes `runc`, the reference implementation of the Open Container Initiative (OCI) runtime specification. `runc` creates the namespaces, joins the cgroup, applies capabilities and the seccomp profile, mounts the root file system, executes the entrypoint, and exits. Kubernetes talks to `containerd` or CRI-O directly through the Container Runtime Interface; `dockerd` is not required.

blocks.text:
#### Containers compared with virtual machines

A virtual machine virtualises hardware: a hypervisor presents virtual CPUs, memory and devices, and each guest runs its own kernel. A container virtualises the operating system interface: all containers share one kernel. The consequences are practical. A container starts in milliseconds and carries no kernel memory overhead, but a kernel vulnerability is shared by all containers on the host, and a container cannot run a different kernel version or a different operating system family than the host.

A **Type 1** hypervisor runs directly on the hardware (Xen, VMware ESXi, Hyper-V). **KVM** turns the Linux kernel itself into a Type 1 hypervisor: the `kvm` module uses the processor virtualisation extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V), and each guest is a user-space process (usually QEMU) whose virtual CPUs are ordinary threads scheduled by the host. A **Type 2** hypervisor is an application on a host operating system (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). Most cloud virtual machines are KVM or Xen guests; a Kubernetes node is therefore often a virtual machine, and the **steal** time reported by the guest kernel is the time its virtual CPUs were runnable while the hypervisor ran something else.

blocks.text:
#### Kubernetes requests, limits and quality of service

A Kubernetes container declares `resources.requests` (used by the scheduler to place the pod) and `resources.limits` (enforced by the kernel). The kubelet translates them into cgroup settings and assigns a **quality of service (QoS)** **class** that determines the kernel out-of-memory score.

rows: Allocation beyond the limit triggers the cgroup OOM killer (exit 137).
The group is throttled for the rest of the 100 ms period.
Relative weight under contention; no cap when the node is idle.
Not enforced as a floor; sets oom\_score\_adj for Burstable pods.

blocks.alt: QoS class Rule (every container) oom_score_adj cgroup parent | requests = limits | Guaranteed -997 kubepods/pod<uid> | (cpu and memory) | at least one request | Burstable 2 .. 999 kubepods/burstable/pod<uid> | or limit set; not equal | BestEffort no requests, no limits 1000 kubepods/besteffort/pod<uid> | Burstable: adj = 1000 - (1000 x memory request / node capacity), clamped to 2 .. 999 | Kernel OOM kill order: highest oom_score_adj first

blocks.text:
The Burstable formula is `oom_score_adj = 1000 - (1000 * memory_request / node_memory_capacity)`, clamped to the range 2 to 999. A container that requests 1 GiB on a node with 16 GiB receives about 938; a container that requests 8 GiB receives 500. The class is a statement about who is sacrificed first, not a guarantee of safety: a Guaranteed pod that exceeds its own limit is still killed by the cgroup OOM killer, because the limit applies regardless of the score.

### Worked trace

The following sequence builds a container without Docker. The root file system is a directory holding `bash`, a handful of utilities and the shared libraries they need (copied with `ldd`). Each numbered step corresponds to a kernel action.

1. `unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc=ROOT/proc --uts --ipc --net --mount` calls `unshare(2)` with five `CLONE_NEW*` flags. Because a new pid namespace applies only to children, `--fork` makes `unshare` fork; the child becomes PID 1 of the new namespace.
2. `--mount-proc` mounts a fresh `proc` file system at `ROOT/proc` inside the new mount namespace so that `ps` reads the new PID table instead of the host table.
3. `chroot ROOT /bin/bash` changes the root directory of the process. From this point `/` is `ROOT`; `/etc`, `/home` and every host path are unreachable by name.
4. The script runs `hostname box1`. The change affects only the new uts namespace; the host keeps its name.
5. `ps -ef` reads `/proc` and finds two processes, PID 1 (the script) and the `ps` itself. The network namespace contains only a loopback interface in the down state, so the container has no connectivity.
6. From the host, `/proc/1275/status` shows `NSpid: 1275 1`, and `/proc/1275/root` resolves to the container root directory: the process is an ordinary host process observed through two views.

A real container runtime adds, to these steps, a cgroup assignment (so that limits apply), a capability bounding set, a seccomp filter, a pivot\_root instead of chroot (to remove the old root from the mount table), and a virtual Ethernet pair connecting the network namespace to a bridge.

All experiments ran as root on the build machine (2 CPUs, 8 GB, Linux 6.18.44, JDK 21, hybrid cgroup v1). Each cgroup used a name private to the experiment, and every process was started with a time bound.

#### A memory limit enforced by the kernel

A memory cgroup was created, limited to 64 MiB, and a C program that allocates and touches 10 MB every 50 ms was started inside it.

blocks.title: hog.c

blocks.code:
$ M=/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/osw_o6
$ echo $((64*1024*1024)) > $M/memory.limit_in_bytes
$ ( echo $BASHPID > $M/cgroup.procs; exec timeout 20 ./hog ) > hog.out
Killed
$ echo "exit=$?"
exit=137
$ tail -2 hog.out
touched 50 MB
touched 60 MB
$ cat $M/memory.max_usage_in_bytes
67108864
$ grep oom_kill $M/memory.oom_control
oom_kill 1
$ dmesg | tail -2
oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_MEMCG,nodemask=(null),cpuset=/,mems_allowed=0,oom_memcg=/osw_o6,
  task_memcg=/osw_o6,task=hog,pid=1809,uid=0
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 1809 (hog) total-vm:74420kB, anon-rss:65024kB,
  file-rss:1640kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:0 pgtables:180kB oom_score_adj:0
blocks.title: Run the allocator inside a 64 MiB memory cgroup

blocks.text:
The program printed "touched 60 MB" and died while touching the next chunk. The usage counter stopped at exactly 67,108,864 bytes, the kernel log names `CONSTRAINT_MEMCG` (a cgroup limit, not host exhaustion), and the exit status 137 equals 128 plus signal 9. The line `constraint=CONSTRAINT_MEMCG` is the decisive evidence that distinguishes a container kill from a host-wide out-of-memory event, which reports `CONSTRAINT_NONE`.

#### A CPU quota and its effect on latency

A CPU cgroup with `cpu.cfs_quota_us` set to 25000 and the default period of 100000 microseconds allows 25 ms of CPU time per 100 ms. The Java program below executes 150 sequential requests, each requiring 10 ms of CPU, and prints percentile latencies.

blocks.title: Lat.java

blocks.code:
$ java -cp . Lat
requests=150 p50=10ms p99=15ms max=23ms
$ echo 25000 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/osw_o6/cpu.cfs_quota_us
$ ( echo $BASHPID > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/osw_o6/cgroup.procs; java -cp . Lat )
requests=150 p50=10ms p99=82ms max=84ms
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/osw_o6/cpu.stat
nr_periods 99
nr_throttled 85
throttled_time 4809441318
blocks.title: The same program without and with a 25% CPU quota (measured on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The median is unchanged, which is why average-based dashboards stay green, while the 99th percentile grows from 15 ms to 82 ms. A request that begins late in a period exhausts the quota, and the whole group sleeps until the next period starts. The counters are cumulative for the cgroup: an earlier 5 second CPU burner had already contributed 47 periods, 36 of them throttled, so the Java run added 52 periods, 49 throttled and 3.51 s of throttled time. The counters `nr_throttled` and `throttled_time` (nanoseconds) in `cpu.stat` expose the effect directly; the incident case studies in this Part use them as the primary signal.

#### What the JVM derives from the cgroup

Since JDK 10 (and JDK 8u191) the JVM reads cgroup limits when `UseContainerSupport` is enabled, which is the default on Linux. The memory limit determines the maximum heap, the CPU quota determines the processor count, and both determine the collector. The experiment varied the limit and quota of one cgroup and ran `java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` `-XshowSettings:system -version`.

blocks.text:
Three rules follow. The effective CPU count is the quota divided by the period, rounded up. The default maximum heap is 25% of the container memory (`MaxRAMPercentage=25`), which wastes memory in a container dedicated to one JVM; for a 256 MB limit the observed heap was 126 MiB, consistent with the larger `MinRAMPercentage` default (50) that the JVM applies to very small limits. The server-class test selects G1 only with two or more processors and at least 1792 MB; a 1 GB or 1.5 GB container silently receives the Serial collector.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: pod killed with exit code 137 while the heap is healthy

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot service with `-Xmx512m` runs in a pod with a 640 MiB memory limit. After a release that added a file-upload endpoint using a Netty-based HTTP client, the pod restarts several times a day. The heap graph in the monitoring system never exceeds 40%.

**Symptoms.** `kubectl get pods` shows `OOMKilled` with exit code 137 and a growing restart count. The application log ends abruptly without a stack trace and without a Java `OutOfMemoryError`. Heap, GC and thread metrics look normal at the moment of death.

**Diagnosis.** The absence of a Java error indicates that the JVM did not die from heap exhaustion. The commands run in order are listed below, together with a reproduction on the build machine in which a program allocates 10 MB direct buffers inside a 160 MiB cgroup with `-Xmx64m`, compared with a program that exhausts the heap.

$ java -Xmx64m -cp . HeapHog
heap=50MB
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
        at HeapHog.main(HeapHog.java:7)
$ echo $?
1
$ java -Xmx64m -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m -cp . NativeHog     # inside a 160 MiB cgroup
direct=130MB heapUsed=1MB
direct=140MB heapUsed=1MB
Killed
$ echo $?
137
$ dmesg | grep 'Memory cgroup out of memory' | tail -1
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 4728 (java) total-vm:2564688kB, anon-rss:162432kB,
  file-rss:21620kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:0 pgtables:556kB oom_score_adj:0

blocks.text:
In Kubernetes the corresponding evidence is `kubectl describe pod` (Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137) and the node kernel log. Within the pod, `jcmd PID VM.native_memory summary` (enabled with `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`) breaks the footprint into heap, metaspace, threads, code cache, GC structures and `Internal` (direct buffers).

**Root cause.** The container limit (640 MiB) was sized from the heap alone. Resident memory of a JVM is heap plus metaspace plus thread stacks plus code cache plus GC data structures plus direct and mapped buffers plus the allocator's own overhead; the new HTTP client used direct buffers that were not bounded by `-Xmx`.

**Fix.** Immediate mitigation: raise the limit (for example to 1 GiB) and set `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m` so that a direct-buffer leak raises a catchable `OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory` instead of a kernel kill. Permanent fix: derive the heap from the limit with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60` instead of a fixed `-Xmx`, leave at least 25% of the limit for non-heap memory, and bound thread counts.

**Prevention.** Alert on `container_memory_working_set_bytes / limit` above 85%, track `OOMKilled` restarts, enable NMT in staging, and load-test with the production limit rather than a larger test limit.

#### Incident: a container with two CPUs and 1.5 GB runs a single-threaded collector

**Scenario.** A service migrates from virtual machines with 8 CPUs and 16 GB to pods with `limits.cpu: 2` and `limits.memory: 1536Mi`. Throughput is unchanged, but p99 latency doubles and GC pauses appear in the logs with a different format.

**Symptoms.** Pause times of 200 to 400 ms during young collections, a single `GC Thread` in thread dumps, and heap usage capped near 384 MiB.

**Diagnosis.** `java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E 'UseG1GC|UseSerialGC|MaxHeapSize'` run inside the pod reports `UseSerialGC = true` and `MaxHeapSize = 402653184`. `java -XshowSettings:system -version` shows `Memory Limit: 1.50G` and `Effective CPU Count: 2`. The reproduction above (limit 1.5 GB gives Serial, 2 GB gives G1) confirms the threshold.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The JVM treats a machine as server-class only when it has at least 2 processors and at least 1792 MB of memory. A 1.5 GB container fails the test and receives `SerialGC`; the heap is 25% of the limit.

**Fix.** Mitigation: add `-XX:+UseG1GC` explicitly (or `-XX:+UseParallelGC` for throughput services) and `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65`. Permanent: set collector, heap percentage and `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount` explicitly in the deployment manifest so that behaviour does not depend on ergonomics, and record the flags in the application log at startup.

**Prevention.** Print `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` into the startup log in CI and compare it between environments; alert on GC pause p99.

### Questions to expect

#### Interview questions and model answers

1. **What is a container in terms of kernel features?** A process (or process tree) isolated by namespaces (pid, mnt, net, uts, ipc, user, cgroup), constrained by cgroups, and given a root file system from an image, usually via overlayfs. The kernel has no container object.
2. **What is the difference between a namespace and a cgroup?** A namespace restricts what a process can see; a cgroup restricts how much of a resource the process can use. Both are needed: namespaces without cgroups give isolation without limits.
3. **Why does a container's PID 1 matter?** The first process of a pid namespace is its init: the kernel ignores signals with default dispositions for it, it must reap orphaned children, and its exit terminates every process in the namespace.
4. **How does a container differ from a virtual machine?** A VM runs a guest kernel on virtualised hardware; containers share the host kernel. Containers start faster and use less memory but isolate less strongly.
5. **What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?** The kernel reclaims page cache first; when reclaim fails, the cgroup OOM killer terminates a process in that cgroup with SIGKILL. The exit status is 137 and `dmesg` reports `CONSTRAINT_MEMCG`.
6. **What happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit?** It is not killed. The CFS bandwidth controller throttles the group until the next period, which raises tail latency; `nr_throttled` in `cpu.stat` counts the events.
7. **What is the difference between requests and limits?** Requests are used for scheduling and set CPU weight and the OOM score; limits are enforced by cgroup files. Equal requests and limits give the Guaranteed QoS class.
8. **How does overlayfs implement copy-on-write?** Reads fall through the layers; the first write to a lower-layer file copies it to the upper layer; deletions are recorded as whiteouts.
9. **Why can the JVM size itself wrongly in a container?** Releases before JDK 8u191 read host resources; later releases honour cgroups, but defaults (25% heap, Serial below two CPUs or 1792 MB) are rarely appropriate and should be set explicitly.
10. **Is a Docker container a security boundary?** Only partially: the kernel is shared, so a kernel flaw or an excessive capability can cross the boundary. Capabilities, seccomp, read-only root and non-root users reduce exposure.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Containers are processes: namespaces limit visibility, cgroups limit consumption, overlayfs supplies the root file system.

- A memory limit ends in a SIGKILL (exit 137) with `CONSTRAINT_MEMCG` in the kernel log; a CPU limit ends in throttling, visible as `nr_throttled` and tail latency.
- The JVM derives heap, processor count and collector from the cgroup; the defaults (25% heap, Serial below 2 CPUs or 1792 MB) should be overridden deliberately.
- Requests drive scheduling, CPU weight and the OOM score; limits are the enforced boundary.
- A container image is read-only; writes go to the upper layer and large mutable data belongs on a volume.

sections.title: Linux Security, Services and Graceful Shutdown

blocks.text:
A production Java service must satisfy two requirements that are often treated separately: it must run with the minimum privilege that allows it to work, and it must start, stop and restart in a way that the platform can predict. Both requirements are enforced by kernel mechanisms (credentials, capabilities, seccomp, signals) and by a supervisor (systemd on a host, the kubelet in Kubernetes). Failures in either area produce incidents that look unrelated to security: refused port binds after hardening, dropped requests during every deployment, or processes that survive a restart request.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Users, groups and root

Every process carries a real, effective and saved user ID and group ID, plus supplementary groups. Access to files is decided by comparing the effective IDs with the file owner, group and mode. UID 0 is special only because the kernel skips most permission checks for it; the privilege itself is decomposed into capabilities, so a process running as root without capabilities cannot perform privileged operations, and a non-root process holding a capability can.

#### Capabilities

A **capability** is one unit of the traditional root privilege. Linux defines about forty; the most relevant to Java services are listed below.

rows: Binding TCP and UDP ports below 1024.
Changing file ownership; bypassing file permission checks.
Sending signals to processes owned by other users.
Attaching to other processes (debuggers, `strace`, some profilers).
Configuring interfaces and firewalls; raw sockets (`ping`).
Raising resource limits; lowering oom\_score\_adj below the current value.
A very large set of operations (mount, namespaces, many ioctl calls); treated as nearly equal to root.
blocks.caption: Capabilities that appear in service and container configurations.

blocks.text: Each thread holds five capability sets, visible in `/proc/PID/status` as `CapInh`, `CapPrm`, `CapEff`, `CapBnd` and `CapAmb`. The **effective** set is what the kernel checks. The **permitted** set is the ceiling to which the effective set may be raised. The **bounding** set limits what a process and its descendants can ever acquire. The **inheritable** and **ambient** sets control what survives `execve`: an ambient capability is preserved across `execve` of an unprivileged program, which is what allows a non-root service to keep `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`.

blocks.text:
#### Seccomp

**Seccomp** (secure computing mode) attaches a filter, written in classic BPF, that the kernel runs on every system call entry. The filter inspects the syscall number and arguments and returns a verdict: allow, fail with a chosen errno, kill the thread or process, or notify a supervisor. A filter is installed with `prctl(PR_SET_SECCOMP)` or `seccomp(2)` after `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` is set, and it can only become stricter. Docker applies a default profile that blocks roughly fifty rarely needed calls; Kubernetes can select `RuntimeDefault` through `securityContext.seccompProfile`.

blocks.text:
#### Mandatory access control: AppArmor and SELinux

Discretionary access control (file modes) lets the owner decide. **Mandatory access control** adds a system-wide policy that the owner cannot override. **SELinux** (Red Hat family) labels every process and object with a security context and allows an access only when a policy rule permits that label pair. **AppArmor** (Ubuntu, SUSE) attaches a per-program profile that lists permitted paths and capabilities. Both confine a compromised process even when it runs as root. A frequent production symptom is a service that works as root on a development machine and fails with `Permission` `denied` under enforcement; the denial is recorded in `/var/log/audit/audit.log` (SELinux) or in the kernel log (AppArmor), and `setenforce 0` should be used only to confirm the diagnosis, never as the fix.

#### Least privilege for Java services

A Java web service needs no administrative capability. The recommended baseline is: a dedicated non-root user; a listening port above 1024 (the Kubernetes Service maps port 80 to 8080); all capabilities dropped; a read-only root file system with writable volumes only for `/tmp` and log directories; `no_new_privs`; and the runtime-default seccomp profile.

blocks.code:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false      # sets no_new_privs
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
blocks.title: securityContext.yaml

blocks.text:
A read-only root file system breaks software that writes temporary files; the JVM writes `hsperfdata` under `/tmp`, so `/tmp` must be an `emptyDir` volume or the option `-XX:-UsePerfData` must be set.

#### systemd services

On a virtual machine, systemd is the supervisor. A **unit file** declares how to start and stop a service, under which identity, with which limits and restart policy. The unit below runs a Spring Boot jar.

blocks.code:
[Unit]
Description=Orders service (Spring Boot)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=exec
User=orders
Group=orders
WorkingDirectory=/opt/orders
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -jar /opt/orders/orders.jar
SuccessExitStatus=143
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
TimeoutStopSec=40
LimitNOFILE=65536
MemoryMax=1G
TasksMax=1024
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/log/orders
CapabilityBoundingSet=

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
blocks.title: orders.service

blocks.text: The directives that matter in incidents are the following. `Type=exec` marks the unit started when `execve` succeeds. `SuccessExitStatus=143` treats the JVM exit status after SIGTERM (128 + 15) as success; without it, every stop is recorded as a failure and `Restart=on-failure` may restart a service that was stopped deliberately. `TimeoutStopSec` is the time between SIGTERM and SIGKILL and must exceed the application drain time. `LimitNOFILE` raises the open-file limit, whose default is far below what a connection-heavy service needs. `MemoryMax` and `TasksMax` apply cgroup limits to the service. The `Protect*` and `PrivateTmp` options construct a restricted mount namespace. Edits to a unit require `systemctl daemon-reload`.

blocks.text:
Standard output and error of the service are captured by **journald**, queried with `journalctl -u orders -f` (follow), `journalctl -u orders --since "10 min ago"` and `journalctl -u orders -p err`. The journal is size-limited (`SystemMaxUse` in `journald.conf`); a service that logs excessively evicts its own history.

#### Signals and the JVM

A **signal** is an asynchronous notification delivered to a process. `SIGTERM` (15) requests termination and can be handled; `SIGKILL` (9) and `SIGSTOP` cannot be caught or ignored; `SIGINT` (2) is the keyboard interrupt. The HotSpot JVM installs handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP: on receipt it starts an orderly shutdown, runs every registered shutdown hook concurrently, and exits with status 128 plus the signal number, so SIGTERM yields 143. `SIGKILL` bypasses all of this: no hook runs, buffers are not flushed and transactions are not closed.

Spring Boot registers a shutdown hook that closes the application context. With `server.shutdown=graceful` (the default is `immediate`) the embedded server stops accepting new requests and waits for active requests, up to `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` (default 30 seconds), before the remaining lifecycle beans are stopped. The configuration is shown below; it was not run on the build machine (no Spring Boot distribution was available) and follows the Spring Boot reference documentation.

blocks.code:
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
#### Termination in Kubernetes

When a pod is deleted, two sequences start concurrently: the pod is removed from Service endpoints (which propagates asynchronously to proxies and ingress controllers), and the kubelet stops the containers. Stopping runs the optional `preStop` hook, then sends SIGTERM to PID 1 of each container, then waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30) and finally sends SIGKILL. Because endpoint removal and SIGTERM race, an application that exits immediately can still receive requests routed to it; the usual mitigation is a `preStop` sleep of a few seconds followed by graceful shutdown.

blocks.text:
#### Why PID 1 matters

In a pid namespace, the kernel applies two special rules to PID 1. First, a signal sent from inside the namespace to PID 1 is ignored unless PID 1 has installed a handler for it (the same rule protects the real init); signals from the parent namespace follow the same rule for SIGTERM, so a shell as PID 1 without a handler never terminates on SIGTERM. Second, orphaned processes are re-parented to PID 1, which must call `wait()` to reap them; otherwise they remain as zombies. When PID 1 exits the kernel sends SIGKILL to every process in the namespace.

A container whose entrypoint is `sh -c "java -jar app.jar"` therefore has the shell as PID 1 and the JVM as its child. Two remedies exist: `exec java -jar app.jar` in the shell form replaces the shell with the JVM, and a minimal init such as `tini` (or `docker run --init`, or Kubernetes `shareProcessNamespace`) forwards signals and reaps children.

### Worked trace

The sequence below follows one SIGTERM delivered to a Spring Boot container whose entrypoint is `exec java -jar` `app.jar`, with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` and a 5 second `preStop` sleep.

1. t = 0: the Deployment controller deletes the pod. The endpoints controller removes the pod IP from the Service; kube-proxy and the ingress controller update their rules over the following one to three seconds.
2. t = 0: the kubelet runs the `preStop` command (`sleep 5`). The application keeps serving requests that are still routed to it.
3. t = 5 s: `preStop` completes. The runtime delivers SIGTERM to PID 1, the JVM.
4. The JVM starts shutdown; the Spring hook marks the server as shutting down, stops accepting new connections and waits for active requests.
5. In-flight requests complete (for example after 1.2 s). The hook closes the HikariCP pool, flushes logs and stops the context.
6. The JVM exits with status 143 at t = 6.5 s. The kubelet observes the exit and removes the container.
7. Had a request run beyond t = 35 s (grace period measured from step 1, not from the preStop end), the runtime would send SIGKILL and the container status would be 137.

The grace period includes the `preStop` time. A common configuration error is a 30 second grace period, a 20 second `preStop` and a 20 second drain, which exceeds the budget by 10 seconds and ends in SIGKILL.

### Hands-on

#### Capabilities and no_new_privs

The tool `setpriv` changes credentials and capability sets before executing a command. The helper script `bind.py` attempts to bind a TCP socket to the port given as argument.

blocks.code:
$ python3 -I bind.py 80
bind 80 OK
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups python3 -I bind.py 80
bind 80 failed: [Errno 13] Permission denied
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups python3 -I bind.py 20601
bind 20601 OK
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups \
    --inh-caps=+net_bind_service --ambient-caps=+net_bind_service python3 -I bind.py 80
bind 80 OK
$ setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups \
    --inh-caps=+net_bind_service --ambient-caps=+net_bind_service grep Cap /proc/self/status
CapInh: 0000000000000400
CapPrm: 0000000000000400
CapEff: 0000000000000400
CapBnd: 000001fffeffffff
CapAmb: 0000000000000400
$ setpriv --bounding-set=-all python3 -I bind.py 80
bind 80 failed: [Errno 13] Permission denied
blocks.title: Binding port 80 under different credentials (real output)

blocks.text:
Bit 10 (`0x400`) is `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`. UID 65534 (nobody) cannot bind port 80, binds port 20601 without any capability, and binds port 80 once the capability is made ambient. Root with an empty bounding set loses the ability, which shows that the capability, not the UID, is the controlling factor. A related observation on the build machine: writing `-997` to `/proc/PID/oom_score_adj` returned `Permission denied`, because the process lacked `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` (bit 24 is absent from its `CapEff` of `000001fffeffffff`); raising the value is always permitted, lowering it is not.

#### A seccomp filter

The program installs a filter that returns EPERM for `mkdir` and allows everything else, then calls `mkdir` before and after.

blocks.title: sec.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -o sec sec.c && ./sec
before: mkdir -> 0 (Success)
after:  mkdir -> -1 (Operation not permitted)
Seccomp:        2
Seccomp_filters:        1
blocks.title: Compile and run (x86-64 only, real output)

blocks.text:
`Seccomp: 2` means filter mode; the field is the quick way to check whether a container process runs under a profile (`grep Seccomp /proc/PID/status`).

#### SIGTERM handling and PID 1

The program registers a shutdown hook that simulates draining for 300 ms and then idles.

blocks.title: Graceful.java

blocks.text: Three launch variants were tested with `unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc`, which provides a real pid namespace on the build machine.

blocks.code:
$ java -cp . Graceful & kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit=$?"
started pid=2498
hook: SIGTERM received, draining in-flight work
hook: drained, exiting
exit=143
$ unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash -c 'java -cp . Graceful; echo "java exited $?"' &
$ INIT=$(pgrep -P $!)        # host PID of the namespace init (the bash)
$ grep NSpid /proc/$INIT/status; kill -TERM $INIT; sleep 2; kill -0 $INIT && echo "still alive"
NSpid:  2532    1
still alive
$ kill -KILL $INIT           # SIGKILL from the parent namespace is honoured
started pid=2
$ unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash -c 'exec java -cp . Graceful' &
$ kill -TERM $(pgrep -P $!); wait; echo "exit=$?"
started pid=1
hook: SIGTERM received, draining in-flight work
hook: drained, exiting
exit=143

#### Zombies when PID 1 does not reap

A Python process as PID 1 of a namespace forks three children that exit immediately and never calls `wait`.

$ unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc python3 -I noinit.py
    PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
      2       1 Z    python3
      3       1 Z    python3
      4       1 Z    python3
      5       1 R    ps
$ unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc python3 -I withinit.py     # same, plus a wait() loop
    PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
      5       1 R    ps

blocks.text:
### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: 502 errors during every rolling deployment

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot API behind an ingress controller is deployed with a rolling update. Each deployment produces a burst of HTTP 502 responses lasting about three seconds per pod replaced, although readiness probes pass and no error appears in the application log.

**Symptoms.** The ingress access log shows `502` with upstream errors "connection refused" or "connection reset by peer" exactly at deployment times; the error rate returns to zero afterwards; the application's own request log contains no failed requests.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `kubectl rollout status` and the event stream confirm that the errors coincide with pod termination. (2) `kubectl describe pod` of a terminated pod shows `Exit Code: 143` or `0`, not 137, so the container exited promptly rather than being killed. (3) The container log's last line is the Spring shutdown message, followed by no drain wait. (4) `kubectl get pod -o yaml` shows no `preStop` hook, and `server.shutdown` is unset (default `immediate`). (5) The timeline in the figure explains the gap: the process exits at t = 10 s, but the endpoint removal reaches the ingress about three seconds later.

blocks.alt: rollout deletes the pod: SIGTERM at t = 10 s and the process exits at once | the endpoint removal reaches the ingress 3 s later (typical): requests in that window fail | Old pod serving requests process gone | Endpoints old pod still listed in Service/ingress removed | Client 200 OK refused / reset: 502 200 | 0 5 10 13 15

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The application stops accepting connections immediately on SIGTERM, but endpoint removal propagates asynchronously. The window is typically one to five seconds.

**Fix.** Immediate: add a `preStop` hook (`sleep 5`) so that the pod keeps serving while endpoints update. Permanent: set `server.shutdown=graceful` with a drain timeout, set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` larger than `preStop` plus drain time, and enable readiness failure on shutdown (Spring Boot does this automatically on graceful shutdown).

**Prevention.** Run a continuous load test against a staging cluster during deployments and fail the pipeline when any non-2xx response appears; alert on ingress 502 counts correlated with rollout events.

#### Incident: zombie processes accumulate in a container

**Scenario.** A service container launches an external converter (`ffmpeg`, `wkhtmltopdf` or a shell script) for every request through `Runtime.exec`, using a shell wrapper entrypoint. After several days the node reports `fork: Resource` `temporarily unavailable` and the pod cannot start new conversions.

**Symptoms.** `ps` inside the container lists thousands of processes in state `Z`, the pod's `pids.current` approaches `pids.max`, and conversion requests fail with `Cannot run program ... error=11, Resource temporarily` `unavailable`.

**Diagnosis.** `ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /Z/'` lists the zombies and shows that their parent is PID 1, a shell or the JVM. `cat /proc/1/comm` identifies the process; `grep -E '^(State|PPid)' /proc/PID/status` for a zombie confirms state `Z`. `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids/.../pids.current` (v1) or `pids.current` (v2) compares the count with `pids.max`.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The converter's children were orphaned or exited while the parent never collected their status, and PID 1 (a shell) does not reap. Each zombie keeps a PID and a `task_struct` until reaped. The JVM reaps children it started through `ProcessBuilder`, but not unrelated grandchildren that are re-parented to PID 1.

**Fix.** Immediate: restart the pod (all zombies are released when PID 1 exits). Permanent: run an init as PID 1 (`tini` or `docker run --init`; Kubernetes `shareProcessNamespace: true` makes the pause container the reaper), call `Process.waitFor()` or `destroy()` for every started process, and set a pids limit that exposes leaks early.

**Prevention.** Alert on the count of zombie processes per node (`node_processes_state{state="Z"}` in node exporter) and on `pids.current / pids.max` above 80%.

#### Incident: Permission denied binding port 80 after hardening

**Scenario.** A security review requires the service to run as a non-root user. After the change the pod crashes at startup.

**Symptoms.** The log contains `java.net.SocketException: Permission denied` (or `Failed to bind to /0.0.0.0:80`) during server start and the pod enters `CrashLoopBackOff`.

**Diagnosis.** `id` inside the container shows the non-root UID. `grep Cap /proc/1/status` shows an empty `CapEff` after `drop: ["ALL"]`. The server property `server.port` is 80. The experiment in the Hands-on section shows the same failure for UID 65534.

**Root cause.** Ports below 1024 require `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`; a non-root process without it receives EACCES.

**Fix.** Immediate: set `server.port=8080`. Permanent: expose port 80 on the Kubernetes Service (`port: 80`, `targetPort:` `8080`); avoid re-adding capabilities.

**Prevention.** Run the container under its production `securityContext` in CI and fail the build on startup errors.

### Questions to expect

#### Interview questions and model answers

1. **What is the difference between root and capabilities?** Root (UID 0) is an identity for which the kernel skips most checks; capabilities divide that privilege into units. A process can be root without capabilities (powerless) or non-root with one capability.
2. **How can a non-root Java process bind port 80?** Grant `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` (ambient capability, `setcap` on the binary, or `AmbientCapabilities` in systemd), or listen on a high port and map it with a Service, iptables rule or proxy. The second option is preferred.
3. **What does seccomp do and how does it differ from capabilities?** Seccomp filters individual syscalls by number and arguments; capabilities gate privileged operations by kind. Seccomp reduces kernel attack surface even for capabilities the process legitimately holds.
4. **What does the JVM do on SIGTERM?** It starts an orderly shutdown, runs all shutdown hooks concurrently, and exits with status 143. SIGKILL cannot be handled, so no hook runs.
5. **Why does SIGTERM sometimes not stop a container?** The entrypoint is a shell that is PID 1 and has no handler, so the kernel ignores the signal. Use `exec`, an init such as `tini`, or a handler.
6. **What is the Kubernetes termination sequence?** Endpoint removal and `preStop` start together; SIGTERM follows `preStop`; SIGKILL follows after `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30 s, counted from the start of termination).
7. **What does exit status 143 mean? And 137?** 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM, graceful). 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL: grace period exceeded, or OOM kill).
8. **What is a zombie process and why is it harmless but dangerous in bulk?** A terminated process whose exit status has not been collected; it uses only a process table entry, but exhausting PIDs or the pids cgroup limit blocks new processes.
9. **What does** `Restart=on-failure` **do in systemd and why add** `SuccessExitStatus=143`**?** It restarts the unit after a non-zero exit, signal or timeout. A JVM stopped with SIGTERM exits 143, which would otherwise count as a failure.
10. **Why set** `no_new_privs`**?** It prevents a process and its children from gaining privileges through setuid binaries or file capabilities, and is required to install a seccomp filter without privilege.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Privilege is decomposed into capabilities; a service needs none of them if it listens on a high port and runs as a dedicated user.

- Seccomp filters syscalls, MAC (SELinux, AppArmor) confines by policy; both limit a compromised process.
- systemd supplies identity, limits, restart policy and journald logging; `SuccessExitStatus=143` and `TimeoutStopSec` must match the JVM shutdown behaviour.
- SIGTERM yields exit 143 after hooks run; SIGKILL (137) skips hooks. The grace period includes the `preStop` time.
- PID 1 ignores unhandled signals and must reap children: use `exec`, `tini` or `--init`.

Earlier Parts explained individual mechanisms: scheduling, virtual memory, locking, file systems, containers. A production incident presents none of them by name. It presents a symptom (latency, errors, restarts) and a clock. The playbook is the method for moving from the symptom to the responsible mechanism in minutes, and from the mechanism to a change that is safe to apply under pressure. It consists of a measurement discipline, a decision tree, a fixed opening sequence, a set of commands whose output is understood field by field, and a short list of tunables that are worth changing.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Methodology: measure resources, then confirm in the application

Three complementary methods cover most services.

- **USE** (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) is applied to every resource: CPU, memory, storage devices, network interfaces and also software resources such as thread pools, connection pools and file descriptors. Utilisation is the fraction of time the resource is busy; saturation is the amount of queued work (run queue length, swap activity, I/O queue depth, pool wait); errors are discrete failures (dropped packets, OOM kills, `EMFILE`).
- **RED** (Rate, Errors, Duration) is applied to each service request path and tells where users feel the problem.
- The **four golden signals** (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) combine both views for dashboards and alerts.

A resource with high utilisation and zero saturation is rarely the cause; a resource with moderate utilisation and non-zero saturation or errors usually is. The method is deliberately mechanical: it prevents a diagnosis from stopping at the first plausible explanation.

The working loop has five steps: state the symptom with numbers (for example "p99 of `/orders` rose from 120 ms to 900 ms at 14:05"), list what changed in the preceding hours (deployments, configuration, traffic, platform), form one hypothesis, test it with a command that can disprove it, and change one variable at a time. Recording each command and result in the incident channel provides the timeline needed for the post-incident review.

blocks.text:
#### The first five minutes

The first five minutes establish impact, scope and the most recent change, take the host-level readings, isolate the failing layer, and apply the cheapest reversible mitigation. A rollback of the last change is usually cheaper and safer than a live diagnosis; the diagnosis can continue on a preserved instance or from collected data.

blocks.text:
#### Capacity planning basics

Three relations explain most capacity questions.

- **Little's law**: the mean number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the mean time in the system (`L = lambda x W`). A service receiving 200 requests per second with a mean latency of 50 ms holds 10 requests concurrently; the thread pool or connection pool must exceed that value with margin.
- **Utilisation law**: utilisation equals throughput times service demand. If each request consumes 8 ms of CPU, 200 requests per second consume 1.6 CPU-seconds per second, which is 80% of a 2 CPU allocation.
- **Queueing delay**: for a single server with random arrivals, the mean response time is `R = S / (1 - U)`, where S is the service time and U the utilisation. At 50% utilisation latency is twice the service time; at 80% it is five times; at 95% twenty times.

blocks.text:
The consequence for the example above is direct: a 2 CPU limit at 80% utilisation yields a mean response of about five times the 8 ms service demand under the single-server model, before any garbage collection or lock contention. Headroom is therefore planned from the latency objective, not from the point at which the CPU graph reaches 100%.

#### Tunables worth changing, and the caution that applies

Kernel parameters are changed with `sysctl -w name=value` for the running system and persisted in a file under `/etc/sysctl.d/`. Each change alters behaviour for every process on the host (or on the network namespace for namespaced parameters), so each requires a stated reason, a measured baseline and a rollback value.

rows: Relative preference to swap anonymous memory versus reclaim page cache. Lowering it (10) on latency-sensitive nodes reduces swapping; 0 does not disable swap.
Upper bound for the accept queue of any listening socket. Kernels before 5.4 defaulted to 128. The application backlog is capped by this value.
Half-open connection queue; raise together with somaxconn for connection bursts.
System-wide open file limit. Per-process limits (`ulimit -n`, `LimitNOFILE`) are usually the binding constraint.
Maximum memory mappings per process; JVMs with many threads or Elasticsearch need 262144.
Maximum PID value; a node running thousands of pods may require 4194304.
Ephemeral ports for outgoing connections; exhaustion appears as `Cannot assign requested address`.
Heuristic overcommit; 2 enforces a commit limit and causes allocation failures instead of OOM kills.

blocks.text:
*Parameters that appear in incidents. The second column is the value read on the build machine.*

Namespaced parameters (for example the `net.*` family) can be set per pod in Kubernetes, but some require the kubelet to allow them as unsafe sysctls; this depends on the Kubernetes version and should be verified before relying on it. Parameters such as `vm.swappiness` are global to the node.

#### Kernel and operating system upgrades

An upgrade changes behaviour that applications depend on without any change to the application. The recurring categories are: the **cgroup version** (v1 to v2 changes file names and, for old JVMs, container detection; see the case study below), the **scheduler** (the move from CFS to EEVDF in Linux 6.6 altered latency characteristics for some workloads), **default sysctl values** (for example `somaxconn`), the **C library** (changes in `malloc` or DNS resolver behaviour), the **JDK container support** and the **file system defaults**. Safe practice is a canary node pool running the new image for a full business cycle, a comparison of `sysctl -a` and `/proc/cmdline` between old and new nodes, a rollback path (the old image remains available), and a staggered rollout with latency and error alerts that page automatically.

### Worked trace

The case: a release changed the pod manifest from `limits.cpu: 2` to `limits.cpu: 250m`. The `/orders` endpoint showed p99 of 900 ms after the deployment. The trace applies the five-minute sequence with the readings from the CPU quota experiment (quota 25000 per 100000 microseconds).

1. **Minute 0 to 1 (orient).** Impact: `/orders` p99 rose from 120 ms to 900 ms; p50 is unchanged at 40 ms; error rate is 0.2%. The only change in the last 24 hours is release 4.12.
2. **Minute 1 to 2 (metrics; values illustrative but consistent with the experiment).** CPU usage of the pod averages 22% of its limit, which seems healthy; the container metric `cpu_cfs_throttled_periods /` `cpu_cfs_periods` is 0.94.
3. **Minute 2 to 3 (host checklist).** `uptime` shows a load average below the CPU count; `vmstat 1` shows idle CPU on the node and no swap activity; `free -m` shows ample available memory. The node is not saturated, which points at a limit inside the pod.
4. **Minute 3 to 4 (isolate).** `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/.../cpu.stat` (v1) or `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat` (v2) shows `nr_throttled` rising by about 9 every 10 periods and `throttled_time` growing by nearly 750 ms per second. A request that needs 10 ms of CPU occasionally waits 75 ms for the next period.
5. **Minute 4 to 5 (mitigate).** Revert the limit to 2 CPUs (a one-line manifest change) and confirm that the throttled ratio falls to zero and p99 returns to 120 ms. The root cause (a cost-saving change applied without a load test) is then written up for the review.

### Hands-on

#### The 60 second checklist on a real host

blocks.text:
- `uptime`: three load averages (1, 5, 15 minutes) count runnable plus uninterruptible tasks; they are compared with the CPU count (2). A value of 2.06 on 2 CPUs indicates full use without a standing queue.
- `vmstat` column `r` is the run queue (saturation of CPU), `b` is tasks blocked in uninterruptible sleep (I/O), `si` and `so` are swap-in and swap-out per second (any sustained non-zero value is memory saturation), `wa` is time waiting for I/O, and `st` is steal time. The first line is an average since boot and is discarded.
- `free -m`: the column `available` estimates memory obtainable without swapping and is the number to alert on; `free` alone is misleading because the page cache occupies free memory.
- The pressure stall information (PSI) files give the fraction of time tasks were stalled on a resource: `some avg10=1.35` means 1.35% of the last ten seconds had at least one task waiting for CPU.

#### Command crib sheet by symptom

rows: A thread with high %CPU whose hex ID matches a `nid` in the dump.
`nr_throttled` rising; threads blocked on one monitor.
RSS above heap plus metaspace indicates native memory.
100% blocks, or inodes, or deleted files still open.
Rising weighted I/O time and `b` greater than zero.
ListenOverflows rising; `Recv-Q` near `Send-Q` on a listener.
Exit 143 versus 137; hook output present or absent.

### Real-world incidents

Twelve end-to-end case studies follow. Each combines more than one layer of the stack and each uses measurements taken on the build machine wherever a reproduction was possible; cases that could not be reproduced are labelled as typical.

#### Case 1: slow API after a release lowered the CPU limit

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot service in Kubernetes was released with `limits.cpu` reduced from 2 to 250m. The service uses Tomcat with 200 worker threads and a Hikari pool of 20.

**Symptoms.** p50 latency is unchanged, p99 rises by a factor of seven, and CPU utilisation relative to the limit looks moderate. Upstream callers log timeouts at the 1 second mark.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `cat cpu.stat` in the pod's cgroup twice, ten seconds apart; the throttled ratio is `delta(nr_throttled)` `/ delta(nr_periods)`. (2) `jstack` shows many threads runnable but not running. (3) A reproduction with a 25% quota is below.

blocks.code:
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/osw_o6/cpu.stat | head -3      # before the Lat run
nr_periods 47
nr_throttled 36
throttled_time 1298169543
$ java -cp . Lat                                         # quota 25000, period 100000
requests=150 p50=10ms p99=82ms max=84ms
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/osw_o6/cpu.stat | head -3
nr_periods 99
nr_throttled 85
throttled_time 4809441318

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The CFS bandwidth controller grants `quota` microseconds per `period`; with 250m the process may run 25 ms per 100 ms, and all threads of the cgroup are stopped when the allowance is consumed, including the JIT compiler and GC threads.

**Fix.** Immediate: restore the previous limit. Permanent: size the limit from measured CPU demand with headroom (see capacity planning), consider omitting CPU limits while keeping requests (weights provide fairness without throttling), and bound the Tomcat and Hikari pools so that concurrency matches the CPU budget.

**Prevention.** Alert on the throttled-periods ratio above 25% for 5 minutes; require a load test at the production limit in the release pipeline.

#### Case 2: nightly batch job evicts the API's hot data from the page cache

**Scenario.** A reporting job reads 40 GB of export files every night between 02:00 and 03:30 on the node that also runs the order API, which reads a 6 GB index through memory-mapped files.

**Symptoms.** API p99 triples during the batch window; the node's disk read rate rises from near zero to 400 MB/s; `free` `-m` shows `available` unchanged because the cache is reclaimable. **Diagnosis.** (1) `vmstat 1`: column `bi` is high and `b` is non-zero. (2) `grep -E 'pgmajfault|pgpgin' /proc/vmstat` twice: major faults rise by thousands per second. (3) Residency of the index file measured with `mincore`; the helper below reports resident pages. (4) The reproduction confirms the mechanism and the remedy.

blocks.code:
$ python3 -I resid.py hot3.dat batch3.dat
hot3.dat   resident  6144 of  6144 pages (100%)
batch3.dat resident 76800 of 76800 pages (100%)
$ python3 -I fadvise.py batch3.dat           # POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED on the whole file
fadvise DONTNEED issued
$ python3 -I resid.py hot3.dat batch3.dat
hot3.dat   resident  6144 of  6144 pages (100%)
batch3.dat resident     0 of 76800 pages (  0%)
blocks.title: Cache residency before and after posix_fadvise(DONTNEED) (real output)

blocks.text: In this experiment the 24 MB hot file was read twice and then a 300 MB file was scanned twice: the hot pages stayed resident, because pages referenced repeatedly are promoted to the **active** list and a streaming scan fills only the **inactive** list. The experiment did not reproduce eviction, which is the honest result: eviction of hot data occurs when it is referenced once per long interval (and therefore sits on the inactive list), when the cgroup or node memory is smaller than the active set, or when the scan itself is mapped and randomly accessed.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The batch job and the API compete for one page cache; the index pages are cold between requests and fall to the inactive list, where the scan reclaims them. Every subsequent index read becomes a major fault served by the disk.

**Fix.** Immediate: stop or throttle the batch job. Permanent: have the batch job call `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)` (or read with `O_DIRECT`) after each chunk; run it in a separate memory cgroup so that its page cache is charged and reclaimed inside its own limit; move it to a different node; pre-warm the index at start (`cat index > /dev/null` or `vmtouch -t`); schedule outside peak.

**Prevention.** Alert on major page faults per second for the API process (`majflt` in `/proc/PID/stat`) and on disk read throughput at peak hours.

#### Case 3: disk fills after a log level change

**Scenario.** To investigate a defect, an operator changes the root log level to DEBUG through the Spring Boot actuator at 14:10. The service logs request payloads at that level to a file on a small volume.

**Symptoms.** At 14:40 requests fail with `No space left on device`; health checks fail; the node reports `DiskPressure`; the pod is evicted.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `df -h` shows 100% used on the log volume; (2) `df -i` shows inode use at 1%, ruling out inode exhaustion; (3) `du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/log | sort -h` identifies the file; (4) `lsof +L1` lists deleted-but-open files in case rotation removed a file that the process still holds. The reproduction wrote a DEBUG-sized line repeatedly to an 8 MB tmpfs inside a private mount namespace.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** An unbounded log volume combined with a verbose level and no cap on total log size.

**Fix.** Immediate: set the level back with `POST /actuator/loggers/ROOT` and body `{"configuredLevel":"INFO"}`; truncate the active file with `: > app.log` (truncation frees blocks even while the file is open, deletion does not). Permanent: configure size-based rotation with a total cap (Logback `SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy` with `maxFileSize`, `maxHistory` and `totalSizeCap`), log to stdout in containers, and set an ephemeral-storage limit.

**Prevention.** Alert on filesystem use above 80% and on `predict_linear` projections of exhaustion within four hours; restrict who may change log levels in production and expire them automatically.

#### Case 4: intermittent slowness on a cloud virtual machine caused by CPU steal

**Scenario.** A latency-sensitive service runs on a burstable cloud instance. During business hours the latency fluctuates without any change in traffic or code.

**Symptoms.** CPU utilisation inside the guest is moderate, yet requests run slower and load average is higher than usual; there are no errors.

**Diagnosis.** `top` shows a non-zero `st` figure; `vmstat 1` column `st` is the same value; the raw counters are in `/proc/stat`, where the eighth value of the `cpu` line is steal in clock ticks. Two samples give the rate.

blocks.title: Reading steal time (real output from the build machine)

blocks.text: The `/proc/stat` fields are: user, nice, system, idle, iowait, irq, softirq, steal, guest, guest\_nice. Here steal is 1480 of 291,615 ticks, 0.5%, which is negligible; the same host in a noisy-neighbour condition would show 10 to 30%, as in the illustrative bar in the figure.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The hypervisor oversubscribes physical cores, or the instance has exhausted its CPU credits and is capped. Neither is visible from inside the guest except through steal time.

**Fix.** Immediate: move the workload to another host or instance. Permanent: use dedicated or non-burstable instance types for latency-critical services, spread replicas across hosts, and avoid sizing thread pools from `availableProcessors()` alone.

**Prevention.** Export node steal as a metric (`node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="steal"}`) and alert above 10% for five minutes.

#### Case 5: connection timeouts from a full accept queue

**Scenario.** During a flash sale, clients receive connection timeouts although the service CPU is low and no error is logged. The load balancer reports failed health checks on some instances.

**Symptoms.** Clients wait the one second SYN retransmit interval and then fail with `connect timed out`; the server access log shows no corresponding requests.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `ss -ltn` for the listening port: `Recv-Q` is the current accept-queue length and `Send-Q` its limit. (2) `nstat` `-az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops`, or the same counters from `/proc/net/netstat`, rise during the incident. (3) A reproduction with a listener whose backlog is 5 and which never calls `accept()`:

blocks.title: Backlog.java

blocks.code:
$ sh nst.sh                       # prints ListenOverflows and ListenDrops from /proc/net/netstat
ListenOverflows 23
ListenDrops 23
$ java -cp . Backlog 5
backlog=5 connected=6 timed_out=14
$ sh nst.sh
ListenOverflows 38
ListenDrops 38
$ java -cp . Backlog 128
backlog=128 connected=20 timed_out=0

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The application accepts connections slower than they arrive, and the accept queue (limited by the smaller of the application backlog and `net.core.somaxconn`) overflows. In Tomcat the backlog is `server.tomcat.accept-count` (default 100) and the acceptor stops accepting at `server.tomcat.max-connections` (default 8192 for NIO).

**Fix.** Immediate: raise `accept-count` and `somaxconn`, and add capacity. Permanent: remove the reason the acceptor is slow (blocked worker pool, long GC pauses) and apply load shedding earlier with rate limits.

**Prevention.** Alert on any increase of `ListenOverflows` and on `Recv-Q` above half of `Send-Q`; load-test with burst traffic.

#### Case 6: thread leak after a library upgrade

**Scenario.** After a dependency upgrade, a service fails after about 40 minutes with `OutOfMemoryError: unable to` `create native thread` while heap use is normal.

**Symptoms.** Thread count in metrics rises linearly; the error appears at a constant thread count; the pod's memory limit is not reached.

**Diagnosis.** `ls /proc/PID/task | wc -l` gives the count; `jcmd PID Thread.print | grep '^"' | sed` `'s/-[0-9]*"/"/' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` groups threads by name and exposes the leaking pool; `cat` `pids.current pids.max` in the cgroup shows proximity to the limit. The reproduction creates threads in a cgroup with `pids.max` of 60.

blocks.code:
$ java -Xss512k -cp . ThreadLeak       # inside a pids cgroup with pids.max = 60
[warning][os,thread] Failed to start thread "Unknown thread" - pthread_create failed (EAGAIN)
 for attributes: stacksize: 512k, guardsize: 0k, detached.
created 39 threads, then: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids/osw_o6/pids.events

blocks.alt: EAGAIN | pids cgroup: | new Thread().start() pthread_create clone() | pids.current = pids.max | pids.max=60 created 39 threads OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread | pids.current=60 pids.events: max 8 | the other 21 tasks: main thread, GC, compiler, signal and VM threads, shell | the error text mentions memory but the limit hit was the task count

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The upgraded client library created an `ExecutorService` per request and never shut it down, so each request left worker threads parked forever. The JVM counts 21 of the 60 tasks in the experiment as its own threads, so the leak reached the limit after 39 threads.

**Fix.** Immediate: restart pods on a schedule while the fix is prepared. Permanent: reuse one shared executor or close the client in `finally`; configure `pids.max` (`podPidsLimit` in the kubelet) to expose leaks early; name pool threads with a factory so that they are identifiable in dumps.

**Prevention.** Alert on `jvm_threads_live_threads` growth and on `pids.current / pids.max` above 70%.

#### Case 7: requests delayed by five seconds because of name resolution

**Scenario.** A service calls an external API over HTTPS. A small fraction of calls takes slightly more than five seconds although the API responds in 100 ms.

**Symptoms.** Latency histogram shows a second mode at 5.0 to 5.1 seconds; CPU is idle; no errors.

**Diagnosis (typical; not reproduced on the build machine, which has no controllable resolver).** (1) `time` `getent hosts api.example.com` repeated shows a 5 second outlier. (2) `cat /etc/resolv.conf` lists two nameservers, the first unreachable, and `options ndots:5`. (3) `strace -f -tt -T -e trace=sendto,recvfrom,poll -p PID` shows a query to the first nameserver followed by a gap of five seconds before the second is tried.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The C library tries nameservers in order with a default timeout of 5 seconds per attempt; with `ndots:5` (the Kubernetes default) an external name is first tried against several cluster search domains, multiplying queries. The JVM caches successful lookups for 30 seconds by default (`networkaddress.cache.ttl` when no security manager is installed), so the penalty recurs periodically.

**Fix.** Immediate: remove the dead nameserver or point to a working resolver. Permanent: run a node-local DNS cache, use fully qualified names with a trailing dot for external hosts or set `ndots:2` through the pod `dnsConfig`, reuse HTTP connections, and set connect and resolve timeouts in the client. (The protocol itself belongs to the companion material on computer networks.)

**Prevention.** Monitor resolver latency (`kube-dns` or node-local-dns metrics) and alert on query failures and timeouts.

#### Case 8: valid tokens rejected because of clock skew

**Scenario.** After a hypervisor maintenance event, one node of a cluster rejects JWTs issued by the identity provider. Other nodes accept them.

**Symptoms.** HTTP 401 from one pod only; log text such as "Jwt expired at ..." or "Jwt used before ..."; the failure ratio is constant for that pod and unrelated to load.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `date -u` on the failing node compared with a reference host. (2) `timedatectl` (NTP synchronised: no) and `chronyc tracking` (typical; chrony is not installed on the build machine) show the offset. (3) The program below reproduces the validation logic for four clock offsets and prints the real decisions.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The node clock was not synchronised after the maintenance event. Spring Security's default JWT timestamp validation tolerates 60 seconds of skew, so drift beyond that fails validation; TLS certificate validation fails for the same reason when the offset exceeds the certificate validity margins.

**Fix.** Immediate: step the clock (`chronyc makestep`) or drain the node. Permanent: run `chronyd` or `systemd-timesyncd` on every node against reliable sources and keep the tolerance small and explicit.

**Prevention.** Alert when the clock offset exceeds 100 ms (`node_timex_offset_seconds`) and when NTP synchronisation status is lost.

#### Case 9: kernel image upgrade changes the cgroup version

**Scenario.** Nodes are upgraded to an image whose kernel boots with the unified cgroup hierarchy (v2) by default. Within hours some services restart repeatedly and the monitoring agent reports no container memory data.

**Symptoms.** Pods running an older JDK 8 build are killed with exit 137; dashboards for container memory go blank on upgraded nodes only.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup` prints `cgroup2fs` on v2 and `tmpfs` on v1; on the build machine the hybrid layout shows `tmpfs` for `/sys/fs/cgroup` and `cgroup2fs` for `/sys/fs/cgroup/unified`. (2) `cat /proc/self/cgroup` lists one line per controller on v1 and a single `0::/path` line on v2. (3) `java -XshowSettings:system -version` prints `Provider: cgroupv1` (as on the build machine) or `cgroupv2`; an old JVM prints nothing and sizes the heap from host memory. (4) `ls /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/` fails on v2.

Check: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** JVMs before JDK 8u372, 11.0.16 and 15 do not recognise cgroup v2, so container support silently fails and the heap default (a quarter of host memory) exceeds the pod limit.

**Fix.** Immediate: pin affected workloads to nodes still on v1, or set `-Xmx` explicitly. Permanent: upgrade the JDK, update agents and scripts, and add the cgroup version to the node pool inventory.

**Prevention.** Run a canary node pool for any node image change and compare `PrintFlagsFinal` output between old and new nodes.

#### Case 10: memory growth and an OOMKilled restart loop

**Scenario.** A service holds a per-customer cache in a `HashMap` without eviction. It is configured with `-Xmx` equal to the container memory limit. Every few minutes the pod restarts; after each restart the cycle repeats.

**Symptoms.** Restart count increases; `OOMKilled` with exit 137; memory graphs show a sawtooth that ends at the limit; the heap-exhaustion error never appears in the log.

**Diagnosis.** The reproduction ran the cache leak (2 MB per 40 ms) with `-Xmx512m` inside a 128 MB cgroup, three times, sampling `memory.usage_in_bytes` every 0.25 s. A histogram of a running instance identifies the leaking type.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The heap maximum (512 MB) exceeded the cgroup limit (128 MB), so the kernel reached the limit before the JVM reached its own, and the unbounded cache guaranteed that it would be reached.

**Fix.** Immediate: raise the limit or reduce the cache by restarting with a smaller cache size. Permanent: bound the cache (Caffeine with `maximumSize` and expiry), set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` below 75 so that the heap maximum is under the limit with room for non-heap memory, and enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` on a volume that survives restarts.

**Prevention.** Alert on `OOMKilled` events and on heap occupancy after full collections trending upward.

#### Case 11: a batch job takes CPU from the API on the same node

**Scenario.** A nightly job and the API run on the same node. The job is CPU-bound and has the same CPU request as the API.

**Symptoms.** API latency increases whenever the job runs; node CPU is 100%; no throttling is reported because no limit applies.

**Diagnosis.** `top` on the node shows the job processes consuming most of the CPU; `cat cpu.shares` (v1) or `cpu.weight` (v2) of both cgroups shows equal weights; the reproduction pinned two cgroups to one core and compared throughput.

blocks.code:
$ # cpu.shares 1024 : 1024
batch iterations=80962
api iterations=81081
$ # cpu.shares 1024 (api) : 128 (batch)
batch iterations=18053
api iterations=144711

**Root cause.** Equal weights give the batch job half of the contended CPU. Weights have no effect when the CPU is idle.

**Fix.** Immediate: `renice` the job or lower its weight. Permanent: give the batch workload a low request (small weight) or its own node pool with a CPU limit, and schedule it away from latency-critical pods using taints and priority classes.

**Prevention.** Separate workload classes by node pool; alert on node CPU saturation correlated with latency.

#### Case 12: rolling restart kills in-flight work because the grace period is too short

**Scenario.** A queue consumer processes messages in batches that take up to four seconds to commit. Every deployment produces duplicate records downstream.

**Symptoms.** Duplicated or half-processed batches immediately after each deployment; pods terminate with exit 137.

**Diagnosis.** `kubectl get pod -o yaml` shows `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 2` (copied from a template for a stateless service). The reproduction below ran a worker whose shutdown hook needs four seconds, first with a 10 second kill delay and then with 2 seconds.

$ timeout -s TERM -k 10 3 java -cp . Batch
worker started pid=8073
hook: SIGTERM, finishing current batch (needs 4 s)
hook: batch committed, offsets saved, exit clean
exit=124 elapsed=7.03s
$ timeout -s TERM -k 2 3 java -cp . Batch
worker started pid=8122
hook: SIGTERM, finishing current batch (needs 4 s)
exit=137 elapsed=5.01s
